children: Emma Tucker
1. FROM MY DESK

With the midterms looming, the vice president is doing some Vance-splaining. When President Trump said he was "proudly banning" certain news outlets from the White House, Vance cast it as a reasonable step to withhold access. When Trump promised Americans $5,000 if they keep Republicans in power, Vance went on Fox News to explain what he meant.

It's part of a broader role the vice president is carving out for himself, smoothing the harder edges on Trump's words or expanding on them, as he reaches out to dissatisfied conservatives. With the coalition that elected Trump in 2024 now fraying, Vance has been traveling the country, campaigning for Republican candidates and appealing to critics on the right.
Natalie Andrews and Philip Wegmann show how Vance is trying to mend fences for the midterms and beyond.

2. TODAY'S HEADLINES

Behind the sudden public freakout over AI ending humanity is a tight-knit subculture of doomers who shaped major labs like Anthropic and are now considering buying land in remote places, among other survival plans, to escape if the technology goes awry.
Boeing has identified a 737 MAX software glitch that could cause an automated navigation feature to fail, prompting concerns about a potential safety risk while planes are landing.
Regulatory pressure to go public has sparked an internal battle at Tata, threatening the future of one of India's most storied companies.
Tariffs and high prices for diesel, gas and fertilizer, along with Trump's plans to import more beef, have soured the moods of America's farmers and ranchers.
North Korea has started practicing swarm attacks that combine unmanned systems with conventional weapons, adopting tactics already used in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Poland and Ukraine are grappling with a renewed feud over World War II massacres of Poles by Ukrainian nationalists, undermining efforts to unite against their common foe, Russia.
3. FROM THE MARKETS

The AI boom's biggest vulnerability isn't IPO delays or rising interest rates, writes columnist Jonathan Weil, but the moment cash-burning startups can no longer raise fresh capital to cover their funding gaps.
U.S. stocks are surprisingly defying a punishing bond selloff that has pushed yields to roughly two-decade highs. Here's what market history says could come next.
4. READ IT HERE FIRST
A scandal inside the Philadelphia DA's office triggers a referral for a federal investigation.

Larry Krasner, one of the nation's most prominent progressive prosecutors, is facing potential legal trouble. It stems from a flawed filing from his office backing a new trial for Dennis Johnson, a man convicted of murder who has maintained his innocence. His public defenders have worked with the Pennsylvania Innocence Project to clear him. The filing was assigned to a prosecutor just four months into the job by a supervisor who allegedly told her, "If it's good enough for the Innocence Project, it's good enough for me." After major errors emerged, U.S. District Judge Paul Diamond found that Krasner embraced a plan to blame the junior prosecutor and warned deputies of "consequences" if they alerted the court to internal discord, reports Scott Calvert. Krasner said he disagreed with Diamond's findings and that he plans to appeal.
A little-known Social Security perk is delivering a financial boost to older families.

As more Americans have children later in life, a growing number are discovering a Social Security dependent benefit that pays children up to half of a parent or grandparent's full retirement-age benefit until they turn 18, or 19 if still in high school. The little-marketed benefit is altering the traditional math around when to claim. Dalvin Brown details how the rule works and weighs the pros and cons for families deciding between earlier payouts and bigger lifetime checks.

6. SEE THE STORY
A hawk named El Charro is Ford's latest employee of the month.

At (Ford Motor's) massive assembly plant in Hermosillo, Mexico, a persistent pigeon invasion was posing a health risk to workers, disrupting daily operations, and threatening damage to freshly painted pickup trucks and SUVs. After fake "predator" eyes and artificial bird sounds failed, plant managers turned to falconry, bringing in a two-foot-tall Harris's hawk. Patrolling the skies above the 12.1-million-square-foot facility, the flying security guard has logged over 300 flights and reduced bird activity by 80%.

Monday: The U.N. General Assembly's general debate concludes in New York.
Tuesday: A status hearing is held in the Lindsay Clancy murder case following this month's mistrial. The Labor Department releases August job openings.
Wednesday: California gubernatorial candidates Xavier Becerra and Steve Hilton face off in a debate. Micron Technology reports earnings.
Thursday: Nike, Accenture report earnings.
Friday: The Labor Department releases the September jobs report.
8. THE NUMBER

The share of all new solar capacity installed in the first half of the year that went to states Trump won in 2024, according to the Solar Energy Industries Association. Those areas also represented eight of the top 10 states for new installations, showing that the solar industry is growing rapidly in those regions despite the administration's disdain for clean energy and a recent bill gutting incentives.
9. AND FINALLY...
Bosses are getting feedback on how to give their youngest staffers...well, feedback.

If you work with 20-somethings, the traditional once-a-year review is quickly becoming a thing of the past. Used to the instant feedback of digital life, many younger employees feel disoriented and anxious when left guessing where they stand. That has managers leaning on consultants and AI bots to adjust their delivery, with bosses role-playing with machines just to learn how to tell a junior employee, "Let's connect."
